titre: Jørn Utzon never saw the Sydney Opera House he designed
accroche: Pushed to resign in 1966, the architect of the Sydney Opera House would never set foot in Australia again, not even for the opening.
contenu_vulgarise:
On February 28, 1966, at noon, the Danish architect Jørn Utzon meets the New South Wales Minister for Public Works, Davis Hughes, in his Sydney office. He has come to demand payment of an invoice for 51,626 pounds, unpaid for four months, and the funds needed to test at full scale the plywood beams he plans for the ceilings. Hughes replies that he cannot decide anything, citing an unfavorable report from the engineers. Utzon threatens to resign. Hughes retorts: “You’re always threatening to resign…” Stung, Utzon leaves the room. The meeting lasts barely a quarter of an hour.

## A decision made in a single evening

A few hours later, Utzon’s secretary hands Hughes a letter in person accusing the minister of having pushed him out. Hughes sees an opportunity: that very evening, he announces to the press that Utzon has resigned, then confirms it to Parliament the next day. The project, begun in 1959 with an estimated budget of 3.5 million pounds, has by then already cost 13.7 million.

The news sets off a mobilization unprecedented for an architect: letters of protest pour in from around the world, and on March 3, a thousand people march past State Parliament behind the architect Harry Seidler and the writer Patrick White to demand his reinstatement. A petition gathers three thousand signatures. To no avail. On April 28, 1966, Utzon and his family embark for Europe at the last minute, barely evading the press. On the way back, they stop over in the Yucatán to visit the Maya temples that had inspired the building’s silhouette. In his luggage, an incomplete set of plans for the third stage: Utzon expects to be called back within two years.

He never will be. The Opera House, whose opening was originally scheduled for January 26, 1963, finally opens only in 1973, under the direction of three Australian architects. Utzon would never set foot in Australia again to see, even once, the building that made him world famous. It would take until 1999 for him to agree to become, from a distance, the monument’s architect again: he then redesigned the former reception hall, reopened in 2004 as the Utzon Room, without ever supervising the work other than from Denmark, through his son Jan.

## What this changes

The Sydney Opera House, now a World Heritage site, owes its silhouette to an architect who never saw it with his own eyes, completed by others by methods he did not choose. The building the whole world photographs as Utzon’s work is also, entirely, the product of a decision made in a single evening by a minister who had only to choose between paying an invoice and winning a battle of wills.

carte.punch: The architect of the Sydney Opera House never saw his building completed, not even from afar.
carte.idee: Pushed to resign in 1966 by a minister after a fifteen-minute meeting, Jørn Utzon leaves Australia and never returns. The Sydney Opera House, planned for 1963, opens only in 1973, completed by others to plans their creator never saw built.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The full account of the break between Utzon and the government, from the institution that now manages the monument.

quiz.question: What immediately preceded the announcement, on February 28, 1966, of Jørn Utzon’s resignation?
choix: A vote of the New South Wales Parliament officially removing Utzon from direction of the site
The collective resignation of all the engineers at the Ove Arup firm, in solidarity with the minister
The publication of an independent audit report judging Utzon’s plans unbuildable as they stood
A fifteen-minute meeting with the Minister for Public Works, during which Utzon threatened to resign
quiz.explication: On February 28, 1966, a meeting lasting barely a quarter of an hour between Utzon and Minister Davis Hughes, over an unpaid invoice and blocked funds, ended with Utzon threatening to resign. A few hours later, a letter from him was enough for Hughes to announce his departure to the press, with no vote, collective resignation, or audit involved.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the amount of the invoice Utzon was demanding at the February 28, 1966, meeting?
choix: 13.7 million pounds, the total cost of the project at that date
3.5 million pounds, the project’s initial estimated budget
3,000 pounds, the amount of the support petition organized in March
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Utzon was demanding payment of an invoice for 51,626 pounds, unpaid for four months, as well as funds to test plywood beams at full scale.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do Utzon and his family do on their trip back to Europe in April 1966?
choix: They stop in New York to meet journalists sympathetic to their cause
They return directly to Denmark with no stopover
They stop over in Western Australia to greet the workers on the site
They stop over in the Yucatán to visit the Maya temples that inspired the building
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On the way back, the Utzon family stops over in the Yucatán to visit the Maya temples that had inspired the building’s silhouette, carrying an incomplete set of plans for the third stage.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Jørn Utzon become, from a distance, the architect of the Sydney Opera House again?
choix: In 1999, to redesign the former reception hall
In 1973, to supervise the building’s opening in person
In 1982, on the tenth anniversary of the opening
Never: he refuses any new commission until his death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1999, Utzon agrees to redesign the former reception hall, reopened in 2004 as the Utzon Room, supervising the work from Denmark through his son Jan.
